reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .507 xSLG tells you this is a legitimate plus-power profile, and when you layer in a 13.2% barrel rate and 49.0% hard-hit rate, the projection's 44 home runs stop looking like an overreach. The tension is the strikeout rate: 26.0% K% with a 34.4% chase rate means pitchers have found a real door, and the xBA sits at .264 because of it rather than tracking closer to the xwOBA. What saves the profile is 11.3% BB%, which is well above average, and 29.5 ft/s sprint speed that turns singles into doubles and outs into stolen bases, the latter projected at 40 even in a full 732 PA season. If pitchers keep attacking that chase rate and he doesn't adjust, you're looking at a high-strikeout slugger with a narrower ceiling; if the walk rate holds and the contact firms up even slightly, this is a middle-of-the-order plus threat with elite athleticism underneath it.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-four home runs at 23 years old is the headline, and the Statcast profile makes it believable: 92.8 mph average exit velocity and a 50.0% hard-hit rate put him in company that genuinely damages baseballs, and an xSLG of .499 says the current .535 SLG projection isn't running ahead of the contact quality. His 11.3% walk rate gives the .362 OBP a real foundation, and an 18.3% strikeout rate that sits below league average means there's no hidden whiff problem dragging against the power. The one live wire is defense: a 1st-percentile OAA is a problem that could push him to DH and clip his everyday value if Tampa can't absorb it. If the glove stays at third, you're looking at a middle-of-the-order cornerstone; if it doesn't, he's still a productive bat, just a narrower roster piece.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The 94.7 mph average exit velocity sits at the 99th percentile, and everything downstream from it confirms that the contact quality is legitimate: a 16.3% barrel rate, 53.6% hard-hit rate, an xwOBA of .375. The catch is the 27.5% strikeout rate, because when you're punching out that often, the bat-to-ball side is always one rough stretch away from pulling the whole line down. What saves it is the .283 xBA tracking right alongside the projection's .284 AVG, meaning the hits-when-he-connects piece holds, and 10.7% walks give him enough on-base floor to keep the .362 OBP from evaporating if the K rate climbs. With 29 home runs and 29 steals baked into the projection, he's one of the few players in baseball where the speed and power numbers are equally credible, and the profile stays whole as long as the strikeouts don't balloon past where they already live.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .471 and the barrel rate at 12.7%, and those two numbers are pointing at the same thing: Stewart squares the ball up with above-average frequency, and when he does, it goes. What's slightly odd is that the hard-hit rate is only 40.0%, which reads below the midpoint of the league, so the damage is concentrated rather than spread across contact. The .346 xwOBA says he's extracting real offensive value from that profile, and a projection of 33 home runs across 706 plate appearances gives it a full-season shape. The whiff (27.6%) and chase (31.2%) rates are the thing to watch, because a pitcher who finds the right sequence could turn that contact quality into swing-and-miss trouble in a hurry, and the .256 xBA already shows the hit tool isn't carrying its weight.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.

His 33.6% chase rate is the one blemish in an otherwise elite Statcast profile, the lever that keeps a true superstar season from being a certainty in any given year. reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The contact and power Statcast numbers pull hard in one direction; the plate discipline numbers pull just as hard in the other. Merrill's .494 xSLG and 49.0% hard-hit rate sit in elite company, and his 29.0 ft/s sprint speed adds a layer most power hitters don't carry, which is how you get a projection of 27 home runs and 27 stolen bases in the same season. The catch is a 36.9% chase rate that lands near the bottom of the league, and a 6.3% walk rate to match, which is why the projection settles at .303 OBP despite the underlying quality of contact. If pitchers can keep working him off the zone and he won't adjust, the power numbers compress and the speed becomes the only thing keeping him from a second-division profile, but if the bat-to-ball quality holds even against aggressive attack plans, an everyday middle-of-the-order outfielder is a real outcome.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: A .412 xwOBA at age 23, with contact quality in the 99th percentile across the board, is not a profile that needs much defending. The argument is simple: Wood chases just 21.4% of pitches and walks at a 16.9% clip, so when he does swing at strikes, he's hitting them at 95.1 mph average exit velocity with a 20.1% barrel rate, and pitchers have no safe quadrant to work in. The one real tension in the profile is a 28.6% strikeout rate sitting at the 10th percentile, a 30.1% whiff rate that signals pitchers can still beat him in the zone, and whether that gap between elite contact quality and below-average contact frequency closes as he ages into his prime or stays wide enough to cap his ceiling. If the strikeout rate drifts down even modestly, the projected .392 OBP with 32 home runs becomes the floor; if it doesn't, the power still plays but the walk rate is doing a lot of the damage-limitation work.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact quality here is almost unfair: a .297 xBA ranks in the 99th percentile, and the 54.1% hard-hit rate backs it up at the 97th percentile, which is why the projection's .287 actual average looks conservative rather than optimistic. At 93.1 mph average exit velocity he punishes mistakes consistently, and the .378 xwOBA suggests the .823 OPS projection leaves something on the table. The whole profile hinges on the 26.4% whiff rate, which sits at just the 36th percentile — if pitchers find a way to exploit it more aggressively, the strikeout rate climbs from 18.4% and the counting stats compress even with the elite contact shape. When it holds, you're looking at a .290-plus hitter with 25 home runs, 38 stolen bases, and the kind of exit-velocity profile that makes every gap dangerous.

reports.name: Jackson Chourio
reports.published_report: The contact quality is loud for a 22-year-old: 91.6 mph average exit velo, a 47.0% hard-hit rate, and an xSLG of .471 that already outpaces what his current .SLG projection asks of him. The problem sitting right next to all of that is a 34.1% chase rate, and until that number comes down, the walk rate will stay thin and pitchers will keep finding the path of least resistance. What he is right now is a five-category contributor who beats you with his legs and his bat when he's on time, and the projection's .288/.344/.486 line looks conservative against a Statcast profile that grades out well above average on everything except plate discipline. If the zone management ever catches up to the raw contact quality, he stops being a very good young outfielder and starts being something harder to plan against.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The contact profile has a wrinkle worth naming: a 31.5% whiff rate sits near the bottom of the league while the .399 xwOBA and .554 xSLG sit at the very top of it, which means he's generating elite expected damage on contact while giving away more swings than you'd expect from a hitter this good. That tension resolves in his favor because a 15.8% barrel rate and 93.2 mph average exit velocity say the contact, when it lands, is genuinely punishing. On the mound, the 2.73 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate against hitters describe a true ace, and 98.1 mph on the fastball is the foundation that makes the strikeout rate credible. The whole profile hinges on health and workload management across both roles, but when both sides are active, the Statcast read is the same in either direction: a front-of-the-rotation starter and a middle-of-the-order bat occupying the same roster spot.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the argument: 95 walks across AA & A+ & A at 18 years old, translating to a 12.7% BB% at the MLB level while the typical big leaguer sits around 8.5%. That kind of plate discipline at this age is what separates profiles that perform from profiles that stall, and the .406 OBP across AA & A+ & A is the downstream proof. The translated ISO comes in at .134, below the MLB mean of .150, so the ceiling here is built on getting on base, running (62 stolen bases across AA & A+ & A), and making contact, not on carrying a lineup with power. If that approach holds and the gap power stays in its current lane, he's an everyday shortstop; if the strikeouts drift up when he faces better velocity, what's left is a high-OBP bench piece with plus speed.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll

reports.name: Gage Wood
reports.published_report: The K-BB% across AA & A is 27%, and that's the number that makes Gage Wood worth watching. He's struck out 139 across 95 innings while walking just 30, and when you level-adjust that profile, the K/9 translates to 9.6 at the MLB level, a full strikeout per nine above where the average MLB arm sits. The concern is the walk rate: his MLB-equivalent BB/9 of 3.3 lands almost exactly at the MLB mean, meaning the command that looks clean in the minors flattens almost entirely once you translate it, and if walks creep even a tick in a big-league zone, the strikeouts have to carry the full load. If the stuff plays up, he's a rotation starter; if the walk rate drifts and the strikeouts don't fully translate, what's left is a depth arm.

reports.name: Ezequiel Duran
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is quietly damning: a .306 xwOBA and a 35.8% chase rate that ranks in the 18th percentile, meaning he's offering at pitches out of the zone at a rate most hitters can't survive. The underlying contact metrics, xBA at .247 and xSLG at .379, sit well below what the projection's .269/.330/.438 line implies, and the gap between what he's actually doing and what he's projected to produce rests almost entirely on whether his 88th-percentile speed keeps inflating his batting average on balls in play and buying him stolen bases. If the chase rate doesn't come down, he's a second-division regular held together by legs, not bat, with a floor closer to a fringe starter getting squeezed out of a lineup than an asset worth 595 plate appearances. The fielding OAA percentile is legitimately elite, which buys him runway, but this profile hinges on discipline improving enough to make pitchers respect him.

reports.name: Nick Gonzales
reports.published_report:
The xBA is 92nd percentile. That single number explains why a guy with an 86.2 mph average exit velocity and a 3.0% barrel rate is projecting to hit .304.

Gonzales isn't hitting the ball hard; he's hitting it where they aren't, consistently enough that the batted-ball model believes him even when the raw contact quality doesn't impress. The projection's .367 OBP and 16.0% strikeout rate cohere: he controls the zone well enough to make weak contact work, and the 28.8 ft/s sprint speed turns a few grounders into hits that a slower hitter simply doesn't get. The whole profile hinges on that contact-placement skill holding at the major-league level across a full 620 PA, because if pitchers start executing more consistently, there's not enough raw power, seven projected home runs and a .395 SLG, to carry the offensive line without the batting average propping it up.

reports.name: Shane McClanahan
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells a story of a guy who is not yet the pitcher he was before the injury: a 4.28 xERA with contact quality numbers that put him in the bottom quarter of the league, and a barrel rate that confirms hitters are squaring him up more than they used to. The 26.8% whiff rate and 31.6% chase rate show the deception is still there, and the 95.6 mph fastball says the arm is alive, but the strikeout rate has slipped to 21.8% and the underlying contact damage makes the 3.36 projection ERA feel generous. If the swing-and-miss profile sharpens as he builds back into full workload, 121.2 projected innings being noticeably short of a healthy ace season, you get the front-of-rotation arm Tampa paid for; if the contact suppression doesn't return with the added stress, what's left is a mid-rotation innings-eater on a short leash.

reports.name: Cade Cavalli
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the engine here — 28.2 K% ranks him with the genuinely dangerous arms in the league, and 206 strikeouts over 176.4 projected innings is the kind of volume that makes a rotation meaningful. The Statcast profile backs the swing-and-miss up: 27.3% whiff rate is legitimately above average, the fastball sits 96.8 mph, and hard contact against him (40.3% hard-hit, 89.1 mph average exit velo) runs below what you'd fear from a guy allowing that much contact. reports.name: Jackson Holliday

The xwOBA is the problem. A 42.2% chase rate, bottom 4% of the league, is dragging his expected production well below what his contact and power numbers suggest he could be, and a 3.1% walk rate is the downstream consequence of that same aggression.

If he can't pull the chase rate toward something functional, the projection's .726 OPS over 407 PA is roughly the ceiling, not the floor, a guy with enough tools to keep a roster spot but not enough discipline to do more than that.

reports.name: Cole Carrigg
reports.published_report: The sprint speed is the most interesting thing in this profile. At 28.8 ft/s, Carrigg runs well enough to make the 12 projected steals feel conservative rather than padded, and it gives his .262/.334/.441 projection a texture that pure contact or power hitters don't have. The power is modest, nine home runs across a partial season of plate appearances, so the profile lives or dies on whether he can stay on base enough to weaponize the legs. If the on-base holds, he's a useful fourth outfielder with real baserunning value; if the .334 OBP erodes at Coors-adjusted league competition, what's left is a below-average offensive profile that speed alone can't rescue.

reports.name: Andre Pallante
reports.published_report: The whole argument lives in one brutal tension: a 4.9% barrel rate and 34.2% hard-hit rate that rank in the 88th and 81st percentiles, paired with a 16.5% strikeout rate that sits in the 10th. Pallante gets weak contact at an elite level and almost never misses bats, a combination that works exactly as long as he keeps the ball on the ground and the defense holds up. His 26.3% chase rate is bottom-decile, so hitters aren't expanding for him; they're just making soft contact when they do swing, which is a thinner margin than it sounds. If that contact-suppression slips even slightly, a 3.73 ERA projection built on 162.1 innings becomes a story about a soft-tosser without a put-away pitch, and the 4.02 xERA is already whispering that version.

reports.name: Eric Hartman
reports.published_report: The 56 stolen bases are the loudest number in this profile, and they're also the most honest summary of where Eric Hartman stands. Across AA & A+, his .456 slugging and .207 ISO look like a power-speed combination worth tracking, but the MLB translation deflates the ISO to .144, right at league average, while his strikeout rate pushes to 28.3% against a league that sits at 22.0%. At 20 years old in Double-A with 583 plate appearances, the athleticism is clearly real and the walk rate translates to a usable 9.5%, so the floor isn't empty. The whole profile hinges on whether the bat-to-ball improves enough to let the speed play regularly, and if it doesn't, the ISO deflation and strikeout load leave him as an organizational depth piece rather than a left fielder who holds a roster spot.

reports.name: Scott Bandura

reports.name: Austin Riley
reports.published_report: The contact metrics are brutal, and they're not going anywhere. Riley's 31.6% strikeout rate sits at the 5th percentile, his xBA is .212, and yet he still makes hard contact on 44.7% of balls in play with a 12.0% barrel rate that grades in the 77th percentile. That's the whole contradiction: elite raw power, almost no ability to put the bat on the ball consistently enough to realize it. The projection's .223 AVG and .664 OPS over 638 plate appearances is the logical result of that gap, a guy who hits the ball hard when he hits it and misses too often to matter the way he once did. Unless the strikeout rate comes down meaningfully, and there's nothing in the chase or whiff profile suggesting it will, this is a fringy regular at a premium defensive position rather than the middle-of-the-order force Atlanta still needs him to be.

Across A+ & A, Parker is drawing 80 walks against 117 strikeouts in 496 plate appearances, a 16% clip that translates to 11.5% at the MLB level, while the 24% strikeout rate here becomes 28.8% in translation, well above what the average MLB hitter runs. That gap, fine plate discipline sitting alongside a swing-and-miss load that outpaces the league at translation, is the whole tension: the .399 OBP and 28 stolen bases paint a table-setter, but the power (.191 ISO here, .126 in translation) and the strikeout rate leave him short of a complete everyday profile. If the walk discipline holds as he climbs and the strikeouts don't worsen, he has a real shot at a second-division regular; if the strikeouts expand against better arms, the walks alone don't carry the profile and you're left with an organizational depth piece, which is exactly what the ceiling says.

reports.name: Michael McGreevy
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost uniformly bottom-quartile: a 5.28 xERA, 17.0% strikeout rate, and 41.6% hard-hit rate against him paint a pitcher who doesn't miss bats and doesn't suppress contact quality either. The one real asset is a 6.8% walk rate, which is genuinely above average, and that command floor is what keeps the projection from matching the xERA. If you believe the 3.85 projection, you're betting that sequencing, defense, and soft contact outcomes regress meaningfully in his favor — a lot of weight on factors outside his control. A back-end starter who could just as easily settle into a swingman or long-relief role if the strikeout rate doesn't climb.

reports.name: Will Warren
reports.published_report: The ERA looks palatable; the contact profile is not. Warren's 44.4% hard-hit rate and 90.9 mph average exit velocity sit at the very bottom of the leaderboard, and the .322 xwOBA with a 4.40 xERA is the truer picture of what hitters do when they connect. The saving grace is 2541 rpm on the fastball, elite spin that keeps strikeout and walk rates near average and presumably generates the weak swings when it works, but it isn't suppressing hard contact at a rate that makes a rotation spot comfortable. If the spin keeps missing bats and the hard contact stays manageable over a full season, he's a back-end starter who earns that 3.91 ERA projection; if it doesn't, the underlying numbers say 4.40 is closer to right, and you're looking at a long-relief arm getting stretched.

reports.name: José Ramírez
reports.published_report: The projection is the dissonance, not the skill set. His Statcast contact profile is genuinely elite, a 13.1% strikeout rate and 15.9% whiff rate that put him in rarefied company for contact quality, paired with an 11.4% walk rate that gives him real on-base foundation. The tension is that 4.0% barrel rate and 88.6 mph average exit velocity, which say the hard contact simply isn't there, and the .688 OPS projection reflects that gap between bat-to-ball and bat-to-damage. At 33, with the speed still grading above average at 27.9 ft/s, the floor is a useful, high-contact contributor who runs, but the ceiling is capped by power that the Statcast profile doesn't currently support.

reports.name: Manuel Pena
reports.published_report: The bat is loud and the profile is narrow. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Manuel Peña is hitting .305/.345/.555 with 31 home runs in 506 plate appearances, and his .251 ISO ranks at the 93rd percentile in the hitter pool. The translation to MLB dims it some: that power likely plays to a .181 ISO, but his 6.4% translated walk rate is thin for a first baseman who strikes out at a 25.1% translated clip, and there is not enough patience in the profile to cushion contact variance. This profile hinges entirely on whether a left-handed first baseman can sustain enough contact quality against major-league arms to stay useful, and if the contact holds he's a bench bat who can do real damage in the right matchup — if it doesn't, the on-base floor is too shallow for a regular role.

reports.name: Mitch Jebb
reports.published_report: The contact is the carrying tool. Across AAA, AA, and A in 2026, Jebb has struck out in just 16% of plate appearances, which translates to a 19.5% clip at the MLB level, comfortably under what most big-league hitters post, and his .277 average ranks at the 80th percentile in the prospect pool. The power is the ceiling question: a .167 ISO in the minors translates to .139 against big-league pitching, meaningfully short of the MLB mean, which puts him squarely in bench-outfielder territory if the bat-to-ball skill is the whole of the profile. Twelve stolen bases add a usable secondary dimension, and a 12% walk rate that translates to 9.9% at the MLB level keeps the .362 OBP from being a mirage, but if that gap-power doesn't firm up as he faces better arms, he's a useful fourth outfielder rather than a platoon piece who can hold a lineup spot.

reports.name: Aaron Ashby

Everything here hinges on whether the strikeout rate bends as he climbs; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench catcher with acceptable plate discipline and middling pop.

reports.name: Steven Kwan
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk profile here is almost comically one-sided. Kwan's 8.5% whiff rate and 12.9% walk rate are both elite, and the .274 xBA grades out in the 85th percentile — he genuinely makes contact at a level that sustains a batting average, and the .375 OBP in the projection follows naturally. The catch is the power, or the absence of it: 83.7 mph average exit velocity and a 0.4% barrel rate sit at the absolute floor of the Statcast scale, which is why the xSLG of .339 grades 11th percentile and the projection has him at four home runs across 644 PA. He is a legitimate on-base asset who will run a solid OBP almost regardless of what pitchers throw him, and the whole profile hinges on Cleveland continuing to build lineups where his .723 OPS projection is a feature rather than a drag.

reports.name: Landen Roupp
reports.published_report: The contact suppression is the whole argument here. A 30.0% hard-hit rate and 86.4 mph average exit velocity put him in genuinely elite territory for keeping the ball soft, and a 5.1% barrel rate backs up that shape. The strikeout profile is ordinary, 21.8% with a 24.4% whiff rate that sits right at the median, and the 11.4% walk rate is what could unravel him entirely, because a pitcher who doesn't miss bats in volume has almost no margin for free passes. The xERA of 3.82 is the honest ceiling: if he commands his stuff well enough to hold that walk rate in check across a full rotation workload, he's a serviceable mid-rotation piece who earns his 165.9 projected innings; if the walks climb, the contact suppression can't save him and the 4.02 projected ERA becomes a floor.

reports.name: Thayron Liranzo
reports.published_report: The walk rate sells the story until you run the rest of the numbers. Across AA & A, Liranzo has drawn 60 walks in 393 plate appearances, a 15% clip that translates to 11.6% at the MLB level, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB norm, real plate discipline for a 22-year-old catcher. The problem is what surrounds it: a .211 average against a .238 BABIP suggests the contact isn't unlucky so much as scarce, and 107 strikeouts at a 27% rate translates to 28.4% in MLB context, where hitters average 22.0%. The ISO is legitimate across the sample, .230 at the minor-league level translating to .165 in MLB equivalent, so the power is there, but a hitter who can't run a BABIP above .238 needs the walks and the pop to carry everything, and if either softens, what's left is a backup catcher profile at best.

reports.name: Roldy Brito
reports.published_report: The .305 average across A+ & A is the loud number, but the translation is where this profile gets complicated. At 19 years old, 41 stolen bases in 553 plate appearances make the speed case clearly — that part doesn't need a translator. What does need one is the bat: the MLB-equivalent K% comes out to 24.6, a tick above where MLB hitters sit, and the translated ISO lands at .108 when the MLB average is .15, meaning the present pop doesn't carry. The .37 BABIP is doing real work behind that .305, and a center fielder who runs like this can sustain some BABIP lift, but the walk rate at 7% translates to 6.4, and that's a thin margin for contact-driven profiles when the strikeouts tick up. If the speed plays in center and the hit tool matures, there's a second-division regular in here; if the contact rate stalls and the BABIP regresses, what's left is a bench outfielder who can run.
